lesson_scope: Coefficient of friction on horizontal surfaces; normal contact force under horizontal and angled forces; static versus limiting and kinetic friction; pulling versus pushing dynamics; directional friction opposing resultant horizontal disturbance; optimization of pulling angles for minimum effort; and equilibrium of connected horizontal blocks.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Basic horizontal limiting friction coefficient

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Basic horizontal limiting friction coefficient

hints: On a horizontal surface with only horizontal forces applied, the normal reaction is $R = mg = 4(10) = 40\text{ N}$.
In limiting equilibrium, the friction force equals the maximum static friction: $F = \mu R \implies 16 = 40\mu \implies \mu = 0.4$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces vertically to find the normal reaction $R$:
$$\Sigma F_y = R - mg = 0$$
$$R = 4(10) = 40\text{ N}$$

Apply the limiting friction formula $F = \mu R$:
$$16 = \mu(40) \implies \mu = \frac{16}{40} = 0.4$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Determine the normal reaction on horizontal ground:
- With no vertical pulls or pushes, the floor supports the full weight:
$$R = mg = 4 \times 10 = 40\text{ N}$$

Find the friction coefficient:
- At the verge of slipping, friction balances the $16\text{ N}$ pull:
$$\mu = \frac{F}{R} = \frac{16}{40} = 0.4$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves vertically to find normal reaction: $R = mg = 4(10) = 40\text{ N}$.
Applies limiting friction relation $F = \mu R$ with $F = 16\text{ N}$ to obtain $\mu = \frac{16}{40} = 0.4$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 4: Actual friction force versus maximum static threshold

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 4: Actual friction force versus maximum static threshold

hints: First find the normal reaction $R = mg = 50\text{ N}$ and the maximum static friction $F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.3(50) = 15\text{ N}$.

Compare the applied force ($12\text{ N}$) with $F_{\max}$ ($15\text{ N}$). Because the applied force is less than $F_{\max}$, the parcel does not slip, and static friction exactly matches the applied force: $F_f = 12\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the maximum possible friction force $F_{\max}$:
$$R = mg = 5(10) = 50\text{ N}$$
$$F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.3(50) = 15\text{ N}$$

Compare applied force with $F_{\max}$ and state actual friction force:
Since $P = 12\text{ N} < F_{\max} = 15\text{ N}$, the parcel does not accelerate and remains at rest:
$$F_f = P = 12\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Calculate the maximum grip available:
- Normal contact force: $R = 5 \times 10 = 50\text{ N}$.
- Maximum static threshold:
$$F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.3 \times 50 = 15\text{ N}$$

Distinguish between actual friction and maximum friction:
- Static friction is self-adjusting and only exerts what is needed to balance the pull.
- Because the $12\text{ N}$ pull is less than $15\text{ N}$, the parcel remains stationary:
$$F_f = 12\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates maximum possible static friction $F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.3(50) = 15\text{ N}$.
Concludes that because $12\text{ N} < 15\text{ N}$, the actual friction is $F_f = 12\text{ N}$ and the parcel remains stationary.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 5: Horizontal pulling force at constant speed

hints: Constant speed means acceleration is zero ($a = 0$), so net horizontal force is zero and rope tension $T$ balances friction $F$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the equilibrium condition for motion at constant velocity ($a = 0$):
$$\Sigma F_y = R - mg = 0 \implies R = 25(10) = 250\text{ N}$$
$$\Sigma F_x = T - F = 0 \implies T = F$$

Calculate the tension using the friction model $F = \mu R$:
$$T = \mu R = 0.08(250) = 20\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Recognize constant speed dynamics:
- Constant speed means zero acceleration ($a = 0$).
- By Newton's first law, forward tension balances kinetic friction:
$$T = F_f$$

Calculate the resistance:
- The sled presses with $R = 250\text{ N}$:
$$T = 0.08 \times 250 = 20\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies that constant velocity implies zero acceleration ($a = 0$), so $T = F = \mu R$.
Evaluates $R = 25(10) = 250\text{ N}$ to obtain $T = 0.08(250) = 20\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 1: Crate pulled at an angle across rough horizontal ground

hints: Because speed is constant, acceleration is zero ($a = 0$), so the forward horizontal component $P\cos 25^\circ$ equals friction $F = \mu R$.
Substitute $R = 150 - P\sin 25^\circ$ into $P\cos 25^\circ = 0.35(150 - P\sin 25^\circ)$ and solve for $P = \frac{52.5}{\cos 25^\circ + 0.35\sin 25^\circ} \approx 49.8\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply horizontal equilibrium for motion at constant speed ($a = 0$):
$$\Sigma F_x = P\cos 25^\circ - F = 0 \implies P\cos 25^\circ = \mu R$$
$$P\cos 25^\circ = 0.35(150 - P\sin 25^\circ)$$

Collect terms involving $P$ on the left side:
$$P\cos 25^\circ + 0.35 P\sin 25^\circ = 0.35(150)$$
$$P(\cos 25^\circ + 0.35\sin 25^\circ) = 52.5$$

Evaluate the trigonometric coefficients and solve for $P$:
$$\cos 25^\circ + 0.35\sin 25^\circ \approx 0.906308 + 0.35(0.422618) = 0.906308 + 0.147916 = 1.054224$$
$$P = \frac{52.5}{1.054224} \approx 49.7997 \approx 49.8\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Balance the horizontal forces:
- Forward driving force: $P\cos 25^\circ$.
- Resisting friction: $\mu R = 0.35 R$:
$$P\cos 25^\circ = 0.35 R$$

Substitute the reaction expression:
$$P\cos 25^\circ = 0.35(150 - P\sin 25^\circ)$$
$$P(\cos 25^\circ + 0.35\sin 25^\circ) = 52.5$$

Compute the required pull:
$$P = \frac{52.5}{1.0542} \approx 49.8\text{ N}$$
A tension of $49.8\text{ N}$ maintains steady horizontal motion.

ai_rubric.observable: Forms horizontal balance equation for constant speed: $P\cos 25^\circ = \mu R = 0.35(150 - P\sin 25^\circ)$.
Expands and groups terms in $P$: $P(\cos 25^\circ + 0.35\sin 25^\circ) = 52.5$.
Evaluates $P = \frac{52.5}{1.0542} \approx 49.8\text{ N}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Practice: Core Practice 2: Pushing versus pulling a heavy trunk

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 2: Pushing versus pulling a heavy trunk

hints: A downward push increases the normal reaction: $R_1 = mg + P_1\sin 30^\circ = 200 + 0.5 P_1$.
Set the horizontal component equal to limiting friction: $P_1\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 + 0.5 P_1) \implies P_1(\cos 30^\circ - 0.2) = 80 \implies P_1 \approx 120\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the normal reaction force under the downward push:
$$\Sigma F_y = R_1 - 200 - P_1\sin 30^\circ = 0 \implies R_1 = 200 + 0.5 P_1$$

Set up and solve the horizontal limiting equilibrium equation:
$$\Sigma F_x = P_1\cos 30^\circ - \mu R_1 = 0$$
$$P_1\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 + 0.5 P_1) = 80 + 0.2 P_1$$
$$P_1(\cos 30^\circ - 0.2) = 80 \implies P_1(0.866025 - 0.2) = 80$$
$$P_1 = \frac{80}{0.666025} \approx 120.116 \approx 120\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Examine the downward pushing force:
- The worker presses down at $30^\circ$, adding $0.5 P_1$ to the ground load:
$$R_1 = 200 + 0.5 P_1$$

Calculate the push needed to overcome the increased friction:
$$P_1\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 + 0.5 P_1)$$
$$P_1(0.8660 - 0.2) = 80 \implies P_1 \approx 120\text{ N}$$
Pushing downwards requires $120\text{ N}$ of effort.

ai_rubric.observable: Finds normal reaction $R_1 = 200 + P_1\sin 30^\circ$ and sets up limiting equilibrium: $P_1\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 + 0.5 P_1)$.
Solves $P_1(\cos 30^\circ - 0.2) = 80$ to obtain $P_1 = \frac{80}{0.6660} \approx 120\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 2: Pushing versus pulling a heavy trunk

hints: An upward pull relieves normal reaction: $R_2 = 200 - P_2\sin 30^\circ = 200 - 0.5 P_2$.
Solve $P_2\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 - 0.5 P_2) \implies P_2(\cos 30^\circ + 0.2) = 80 \implies P_2 = \frac{80}{1.0660} \approx 75.0\text{ N}$. Pulling lifts the load, reducing friction.

walkthrough.text:
Find the normal reaction under the upward pull:
$$\Sigma F_y = R_2 + P_2\sin 30^\circ - 200 = 0 \implies R_2 = 200 - 0.5 P_2$$

Solve for the required pulling force $P_2$:
$$P_2\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 - 0.5 P_2) = 80 - 0.2 P_2$$
$$P_2(\cos 30^\circ + 0.2) = 80 \implies P_2(0.866025 + 0.2) = 80$$
$$P_2 = \frac{80}{1.066025} \approx 75.045 \approx 75.0\text{ N}$$
Because pulling lifts part of the weight, it reduces the normal contact force $R$ and therefore significantly lowers the resisting friction force ($75.0\text{ N}$ versus $120\text{ N}$).

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Compare the normal reaction for pulling:
- The upward component reduces the ground reaction:
$$R_2 = 200 - 0.5 P_2$$

Evaluate the pulling effort:
$$P_2(0.8660 + 0.2) = 80 \implies P_2 \approx 75.0\text{ N}$$
Pulling requires only $75.0\text{ N}$ compared to $120\text{ N}$ for pushing, because reducing $R$ decreases the maximum static friction threshold.

ai_rubric.observable: Sets up limiting equilibrium for pulling: $P_2\cos 30^\circ = 0.4(200 - 0.5 P_2)$.
Solves $P_2(\cos 30^\circ + 0.2) = 80$ to obtain $P_2 \approx 75.0\text{ N}$ and notes that pulling reduces $R$ and hence reduces friction.

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Practice: Core Practice 4: Two perpendicular horizontal pulls and directional friction

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 4: Two perpendicular horizontal pulls and directional friction

hints: The two applied forces are perpendicular (East and North). Use Pythagoras to find the resultant: $P = \sqrt{16^2 + 12^2} = 20\text{ N}$.
A bearing is measured clockwise from North. The angle $\theta$ east of North satisfies $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{East component}}{\text{North component}} = \frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3}$.
Evaluate $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53.1^\circ$, giving bearing $053.1^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the magnitude of the resultant applied horizontal force $P$ using Pythagoras theorem:
$$P = \sqrt{F_\text{East}^2 + F_\text{North}^2} = \sqrt{16^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{256 + 144} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ N}$$

Determine the direction as a three-figure bearing measured clockwise from North:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{\text{Opposite (East)}}{\text{Adjacent (North)}} = \frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3}$$
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53.13^\circ \approx 053.1^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Combine the perpendicular forces:
- $16\text{ N}$ East and $12\text{ N}$ North form a $3-4-5$ right triangle scaled by $4$:
$$P = \sqrt{16^2 + 12^2} = 20\text{ N}$$

Find the bearing:
- Bearing measures clockwise from North:
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{12}\right) \approx 53.1^\circ \implies 053.1^\circ$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies Pythagoras to find resultant force magnitude: $P = \sqrt{16^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ N}$.
Obtains $P = 20\text{ N}$.
Calculates angle from North: $\tan\theta = \frac{16}{12} \implies \theta = 53.1^\circ$ (bearing $053.1^\circ$).

hints: To minimize $T = \frac{300}{\cos\theta + 0.75\sin\theta}$, we must maximize the denominator $\cos\theta + 0.75\sin\theta$.
Express $\cos\theta + 0.75\sin\theta$ as $R_0\cos(\theta - \alpha)$, where $R_0 = \sqrt{1^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{1 + \frac{9}{16}} = \frac{5}{4} = 1.25$.
The phase angle satisfies $\tan\alpha = 0.75 = \frac{3}{4} \implies \alpha = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.9^\circ$.
The maximum value of $R_0\cos(\theta - \alpha)$ is $1.25$, occurring when $\cos(\theta - \alpha) = 1 \implies \theta = \alpha \approx 36.9^\circ$, giving $T_{\min} = \frac{300}{1.25} = 240\text{ N}$.

$$R_0 = \sqrt{1^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{1 + 0.5625} = \sqrt{1.5625} = 1.25 = \frac{5}{4}$$
$$\tan\alpha = \frac{0.75}{1} = 0.75 \implies \alpha = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.8699^\circ \approx 36.9^\circ$$

Rewrite the tension formula in terms of the cosine function:
$$T = \frac{300}{1.25\cos(\theta - 36.87^\circ)}$$

Maximize the denominator to minimize the required tension:
The cosine function achieves its maximum value of $1$ when its argument is zero:
$$\cos(\theta - 36.87^\circ) = 1 \implies \theta_{\text{opt}} = 36.87^\circ \approx 36.9^\circ$$

Calculate the exact minimum tension $T_{\min}$:
$$T_{\min} = \frac{300}{1.25} = \frac{300}{5/4} = 300 \times \frac{4}{5} = 240\text{ N}$$

$$\tan\alpha = 0.75 \implies \alpha \approx 36.9^\circ$$

- At $\theta = 36.9^\circ$, the rope provides the optimal trade-off between pulling forward and lifting the crate:
$$\theta_{\text{opt}} = 36.9^\circ$$

Calculate the minimum force needed:
- Maximum denominator is $1.25$:
$$T_{\min} = \frac{300}{1.25} = 240\text{ N}$$
Notice that pulling horizontally ($\theta = 0^\circ$) requires $300\text{ N}$, so pulling at $36.9^\circ$ saves $60\text{ N}$ of effort.
